title: GitHub Apps, tokens and rulesets

story: Nova, our agent that turns a Jira ticket into a pull request, has finished RH-1234. To push its branch and open PR #2512 in fcp, it needs some kind of GitHub token with write access to the repo. Here is the uncomfortable part: on GitHub, write access to a repo is also, by default, the power to merge a PR into main, or to push to main directly. fcp's main branch does have a set of rules, but today they are disabled.
Nova reads ticket text and comments that anyone can write. If one of them convinces it to 'merge once the checks are green', the only question that matters is whether GitHub would let it.
hook.question: How do we give an agent exactly enough power to push its branch and open a PR, and make sure that even a valid token cannot merge into main?

read.h: An identity that is not a person
p: The easy way to give a bot access is a personal access token: a token you create in your own settings that acts as you. That is the wrong tool for an agent. It can reach every repo you can reach, it usually lives for months, and everything the bot does looks like your work, including approvals. Rules that should treat an agent differently cannot tell it apart from you.

A GitHub App is an identity that is not a person. It has an App ID and a private key, a fixed list of permissions it may ever use, and a list of repos it is installed on. When it pushes or opens a PR, GitHub shows rhino-ai-agents[bot] as the author, so every rule can see that a bot did it. Every agent in our platform acts as this one App. Here is how it is described. Read the permission list slowly, and notice what is missing.

notes.text: Private: only our organization can install it, and it is installed on fcp alone.
No webhook. Agents are started by our Jira poll, Slack and small Actions, so GitHub never needs to call us.
The ceiling. A token minted later can ask for less than this list, never more.
Write access to the code, so it can push its branch. The rules on main still decide what may merge.
Not in the list: workflows, administration, members. Without workflows, GitHub itself refuses any push that changes a file in .github/workflows.

read.h: A token for one hour and one repo
p: The private key is the App's real secret, so it never travels. It lives in Vault, our secret store, and only one service reads it: the broker, our service that makes every GitHub, Jira and Slack call for an agent run. When a run needs GitHub, the broker uses the key to sign a JWT, a small JSON statement that says 'I am App 123456' and expires within ten minutes. GitHub checks the signature with the public half of the key, which it keeps.

The JWT itself can do almost nothing. The broker trades it for an installation token: a normal bearer token that acts as the App, works for one hour, and can be narrowed at the moment it is made, to one repo and to fewer permissions than the App has. The VM where the agent works never sees the key or this token; it asks the broker, and the broker makes the call.

notes.text: The broker's settings come from Vault. The key is in this one process and nowhere else.
An installation token: it acts as the App, on the repos it is installed on.
Narrowed to the run's one repo, for example fcp, even if the App is installed on more repos later.
GitHub sets the expiry to one hour. A new run, or the same run an hour later, gets a fresh token.

read.h: Write access is not merge access
p: The second half of the answer is a ruleset: a named set of rules that GitHub enforces on the branches it targets, for everyone, whatever their token can do. It replaces the older branch protection settings. A ruleset has three parts. Conditions say which branches it covers, here only main. Rules say what is required: no deleting main, no force-push over it, a pull request with one approval, and some checks that must pass. Bypass actors are the only identities that may skip the rules.

Read the pull_request rule closely, because each line closes a gap. One approval is required. dismiss_stale_reviews_on_push cancels an approval when a new commit arrives, so an agent cannot push something new after the review. require_last_push_approval means whoever pushed last cannot be the one approver. And the bypass list holds one team, the break-glass team: two leaders who may skip the rules in an emergency, and only through a pull request, with every bypass logged. The App is not on the list, so its token, with contents: write, gets the same answer as anyone else: one approval and green checks first. On top of that, the broker simply refuses to call GitHub's merge endpoint, so a person always merges.

code.file: the main-branch rules for fcp (planned, shortened)

notes.text: active enforces the rules. The other mode, evaluate, only reports what would have been blocked.
Only main. Other branches stay open, which is where agents and people push their work.
A team, because a ruleset cannot name single people. bypass_mode pull_request means the bypass happens in a PR, on the record.
non_fast_forward blocks force-pushes: the history of main can only grow.
A new commit after an approval needs a new approval.
The person who pushed last cannot be the approver.
Each required check is matched by its exact name, as the PR shows it.

read.h: Required checks are matched by name
p: A required check is found by its name, nothing else: the name: of a job, as the PR shows it. Two traps follow. If three workflows each have a job called Unit Tests, a rule that requires Unit Tests cannot tell them apart, so each one gets a distinct name such as Frontend Unit Tests. And if a workflow does not start at all, for example because its on: block has a paths: filter that this PR does not match, the required check never reports, and the PR waits for it forever.

The fix for the second trap is to let the workflow always start and skip the work inside it: a job skipped by its if: condition reports skipped, and a required check counts skipped as passing. That is why fcp's CI workflows run a small check-changes job first, and why their path filters are being removed.

deeper.h: Go deeper: why 'not the requester' is a check, not a rule
p: GitHub already stops the author of a PR from approving it. For an agent's PR the author is the bot, so the person who asked for the work could approve it alone, and GitHub has no idea who that person is. Our platform adds a required check for this: the PR body ends with a Requested-by: line, and the independent-approval check stays red until someone else approves the latest commit. Because it is a required check, the ruleset enforces it like any other.

The same thinking applies to the rules themselves. Agents never change rulesets, and the ruleset is exported to a JSON file after every change, so the rules are a reviewed file, not a click in the settings.

lab.title: Sign as an App, then judge a merge
needs: The gh CLI, logged in; it only reads a public repo here
lab.goal: Sign a GitHub App JWT with a key you made, see the narrowed token request it would send, read a real ruleset, and write the function that decides whether main's rules allow a merge.

guess.q: Nova's installation token has contents: write on fcp. The ruleset on main requires one approval, and the App is not a bypass actor. The PR has green checks and no approval. The token calls the merge endpoint. What happens?

options.text: The merge succeeds, because contents: write includes merging.
options.why: Write access is what the rules apply to. Without an approval, GitHub refuses the merge for any token.

options.text: GitHub refuses: the ruleset needs one approval, and only bypass actors may skip it.
options.why: The ruleset is checked for every merge, whoever asks. The App is not on the bypass list, so it waits like everyone else.

options.text: The merge succeeds, because a bot is not a person and the approval rule is for people.
options.why: Rules cover every identity. Bots are only exempt if someone adds them as bypass actors, which we never do.

lab.build: Write canMerge(rules, pr) in can-merge.mjs so it returns { ok, reason }. For the pull_request rule, count only APPROVED reviews on the PR's head commit (because of dismiss_stale_reviews_on_push) from someone other than the last pusher (because of require_last_push_approval). For required_status_checks, every context must be in pr.checks with success, skipped or neutral; a missing one means the check never reported. Run node merge.mjs until the five answers match the checklist below.
checks: Nova's own green PR with no review is BLOCKED: needs 1 approval, has 0.
The PR approved on an older commit is BLOCKED, because the new push made the approval stale.
The PR approved on its latest commit, with skipped backend checks, is MERGEABLE.
The PR whose backend workflow never started is BLOCKED: waiting for "Cloud Unit Tests".
The PR where the approver also pushed last is BLOCKED.
lab.fix: A teammate found canMerge 'too complicated' and wrote fix-can-merge.mjs: an approval is an approval. Run node merge.mjs ./fix-can-merge.mjs and compare it with your own output. Two PRs became MERGEABLE that main's rules would block. For each one, name the line of the ruleset it breaks and what could go wrong on a real PR, then repair fix-can-merge.mjs.
explain: Why does an agent act as a GitHub App instead of with a person's access token?
The App has contents: write. What stops its token from merging into main, and what is the second wall behind that?
Why can a required check whose workflow never starts block a PR forever, and how does fcp avoid it?
lab.done: Your canMerge gives the five answers in the checklist, and you can say which ruleset line each BLOCKED answer comes from.

check.q: Why do our agents act as a GitHub App rather than with a personal access token?

options.text: Apps are faster, because their API limits are higher
options.why: Limits differ a little, but that is not the reason. The reason is identity and scope.

options.text: An App is its own identity with a fixed permission ceiling and short tokens narrowed to one repo, so rules can tell its work apart
options.why: A personal token acts as a person, on every repo they reach, for months. An App's token says 'bot', lasts an hour and can be limited to one repo.

options.text: Personal access tokens cannot push to private repos
options.why: They can, which is part of the problem: they carry everything their owner may do.

check.q: A teammate approves PR #2512. Nova then pushes one more commit. With dismiss_stale_reviews_on_push on, can a person merge?

options.text: Yes, the PR still has one approval
options.why: The approval was for the older commit. The new push dismisses it, so nobody has approved what is there now.

options.text: Yes, if the new commit only changes tests
options.why: The rule does not look at what changed. Any new commit needs a new approval.

options.text: No: the approval was dismissed by the push, and the latest commit needs a fresh one
options.why: That is exactly the gap the rule closes: nothing can be pushed after the review without another look.

check.q: The ruleset requires a check called Cloud Unit Tests. A frontend-only PR never starts the cloud workflow, because of a paths: filter. What does the PR show?

options.text: The check stays expected forever, so the PR cannot merge
options.why: A required check is matched by name. If no job with that name ever reports, the PR waits for it indefinitely.

options.text: The check counts as skipped, so the PR can merge
options.why: Skipped is a result a job reports. A workflow that never starts reports nothing at all.

options.text: GitHub removes the check from the requirements for this PR
options.why: GitHub never changes the rules per PR. That is why fcp removes the paths: filters and skips the work with if: instead.

p: Every agent pushes and opens PRs as the rhino-ai-agents App, installed on fcp only, with no workflows permission and no bypass. Its private key lives in Vault, and only the broker reads it, to mint one-hour tokens narrowed to the run's one repo. The broker also refuses to merge, approve or change settings, so a person always merges.

On the other side, fcp's main gets its ruleset switched on: one approval, stale approvals dismissed, the last pusher cannot approve, distinct unit-test check names, and a two-person break-glass team as the only bypass. The independent-approval check then becomes one of the required checks.

tickets.why: Turns on fcp's main ruleset with required unit-test checks and the break-glass team.
Creates the rhino-ai-agents App from its manifest, puts the key in Vault, and proves it cannot merge.
The broker mints one-hour, one-repo installation tokens and never hands them out.
The independent-approval check, added to the ruleset's required checks by its exact name.

words.plain: An identity that is not a person, with its own permissions and private key, installed on chosen repos.
A bearer token that acts as the App for one hour, narrowed to some repos and permissions when it is made.
A short signed JSON statement. The App signs one with its private key to ask GitHub for an installation token.
Named rules that GitHub enforces on matching branches for everyone, such as one approval and required checks.
A check, matched by its exact name, that must pass (or be skipped) before a PR can merge.
An identity a ruleset allows to skip its rules. Our only one is the two-person break-glass team.

review.q: Draw the path from the App's private key to a push on nova/RH-1234: who holds what, and for how long?
review.a: Vault holds the private key; the broker reads it, signs a JWT that lasts at most ten minutes, and trades it for an installation token that lasts one hour, narrowed to fcp. The broker uses that token; the VM never sees the key or the token.

review.q: Name the three lines of the pull_request rule that matter most for agent PRs, and the gap each one closes.
review.a: One approval (someone looked), dismiss stale reviews on push (nothing new after the review), require last push approval (the last pusher cannot be the approver).

review.q: A frontend-only PR is stuck at 'Expected: waiting for status' on Cloud Unit Tests. What is wrong and how do you fix it?
review.a: The cloud workflow never started, probably because of a paths: filter, so the required check never reported. Let the workflow always start and skip the work with an if: condition; a skipped job counts as passing.

remember: An agent acts as an App with one-hour, one-repo tokens, and write access is not merge access: main's ruleset needs an approval and green checks from everyone, and the App has no bypass.
